arc.scene1_hook: A figure pushes a massive boulder up a steep hill. Sweat drops fall. The boulder is enormous, the hill endless. We've all seen this image — eternal punishment, futile labor. But as the camera slowly moves to the figure's face... they're smiling. Not grimacing. Smiling. Not because they found a reason for the boulder. Because they stopped needing one. Title pill: "SISYPHUS WAS SMILING".
arc.scene2_mystery: Pull back to show the full journey. Layer by layer, the philosophical path unfolds as a winding mountain path. Signposts mark each station: "NAIVE BELIEF" (bottom, warm glow), "SOCIAL CRITIQUE" (middle, yellow caution), "NIHILISM" (dark cave), "EXISTENTIALISM" (personal torch lit), "TAO" (river flowing). At the very top: a question mark. Having peeled back every layer — acceptance, critique, refusal, reclamation, surrender — you arrive at a strange place. What's left?
arc.scene3_wrong_answer: The assumption: the point of the journey is to find THE answer. A treasure chest sits at the top of the mountain, glowing. "THE MEANING OF LIFE" label. Every philosophy was just trying to crack it open — find the one true metric, the real success, the cosmic answer. The figure climbs toward the chest expectantly. Nihilism said the chest is empty. Existentialism said you fill it yourself. But everyone assumes there's supposed to be something IN the chest. That's the wrong frame entirely.
arc.scene4_contradiction: The treasure chest opens — and inside is a mirror. The figure sees themselves, mid-climb, sweating, alive. The mirror cracks the assumption: there was never something to find. The absurd hero doesn't deny the universe offers no validation. Doesn't pretend personal metrics are cosmically sanctioned. Sees clearly that ALL measurement is human, ALL meaning is constructed, ALL success is a story. And picks up the rock anyway. The chest dissolves. The boulder remains. But the figure's posture changes — from straining to carrying. From burden to dance.
arc.scene5_proof: The figure with the boulder, now smiling, is shown alongside all the previous philosophical positions. Each one tried to solve "the boulder problem": naive belief said the boulder has meaning, nihilism said drop it, existentialism said name it yourself. But the absurdist does something different — they stop asking what the boulder means. A defiance meter fills not with answers but with aliveness. "Not because the task has meaning. Because she is alive, and alive is what she has." The smile isn't relief or denial. It's defiance so complete it circles back to joy.
arc.scene6_betrayal: The hill reveals itself as circular — Sisyphus reaches the top and the boulder rolls back down. He walks down after it. And here's the gut punch: he's not defeated. He's not enlightened. He's not performing. He is simply, fully, completely doing the thing. The elaborate philosophical apparatus — deconstruction, critique, reclamation, surrender, rebellion — was the long way around to something a child building a tower already knew. But the long way around was necessary. You can't skip to the smile. You have to earn it by seeing everything clearly first.

tts_script: Having peeled back every layer — naive acceptance, social critique, nihilistic refusal, existential reclamation — you arrive at a strange place. You arrive at laughter. Not bitter laughter. The laugh of someone who has seen the whole elaborate machinery of success for what it is, and who now, with full knowledge, chooses to live anyway. The absurd hero sees clearly that all measurement is human, all meaning is constructed, all success is a story we tell. And she picks up the rock and carries it up the hill again. Not because the task has meaning. Because she is alive, and alive is what she has. Imagine Sisyphus smiling. Not because he found a reason for the boulder. Because he stopped needing one.
